newsitem.title: ITALY: Alitalia accuses EU commission of prejudice.
newsitem.headline: Alitalia accuses EU commission of prejudice.

text.p: Debt-ridden Italian airline Alitalia said on Wednesday it would press ahead with a rescue plan aimed at bringing the firm back to profit despite criticism of the project by the European Commission.

Alitalia managing director Domenico Cempella said in a statement that it was too late to change the plan and accused the commission of "a serious and prejudiced attitude" against the state-controlled airline.
The European Commission said it had sent a letter to the Italian government suggesting changes to plans to inject fresh funds into struggling Alitalia. It gave no further details.

Italy requested EU permission last year for a capital injection worth some 3.3 trillion lire ($1.9 billion) into Alitalia and the government has already authorised state holding IRI to hand over 1.5 trillion lire of the funds.

"We cannot accept at this point requests for further changes to a plan which we believe in and which is bringing the company back to the path of strong recovery," Cempella said in a speech to Alitalia directors which was released to the media.

It was the second time in a day that Italy had clashed with Brussels. Earlier, Prime Minister Romano Prodi slammed a Commission report questioning whether Rome would make the grade for the European single currency as "incomprehensible".

Alitalia, which chalked up its ninth straight year of losses in 1996, agreed to a rescue package with unions last June after months of bitter battle over plans to slash hefty personnel costs and boost productivity.
Under the terms of the deal, between 20-30 percent of the group's shares will be reserved for employees after the firm's recapitalisation and eventual privatisation.
Private sector competitors, including British Airways, complained about provisions for government money to be pumped into the struggling group.

Cempella said the EU Transport Commission had already told the company to alter some of its proposals -- forcing the group to shed 14 aircraft in 1997 and reduce its overall fleet size to 158 by the year 2000 instead of the planned 172.
In addition, Alitalia has accepted a Commission request to reduce the size of the capital increase to 2.8 trillion lire.
But Cempella said on Wednesday that the latest Commission doubts were unacceptable.

"We do not understand how the Commission can express perplexity on a recapitalisation plan that fully conforms to the needs of the Alitalia plan, which is, and must remain, a plan for the relaunch of the company and not for its marginalisation," Cempella said.
Unions on Wednesday asked for "an urgent meeting" with Prime Minister Prodi in the wake of the Commission's criticisms.
In a statement, the unions said they were: "deeply worried by the situation regarding the Alitalia plan and the European Commission." $1 = 1,705 lire
